source_text: Sed, ut diximus, eadem dementia est, cum confitentur quidem nihil apostolos ignorasse, nec diversa inter se praedicasse, non tamen omnia volunt illos omnibus revelasse, quaedam enim palam et universis, quaedam secreto et paucis demandasse, quia et hoc verbo usus est Paulus ad Timotheum, O Timothee, depositum custodi, et rursum, Bonum depositum serva. Quod hoc depositum est, tam tacitum, ut alterius doctrinae deputetur? An illius denuntiationis de qua ait, Hanc denuntiationem commendo apud te, filiole Timothee? item illius praecepti de quo ait, Denuntio tibi ante deum, qui vivificat omnia, et Iesum Christum, qui testatus est sub Pontio Pilato bonam confessionem, custodias praeceptum? Quod autem praeceptum et quae denuntiatio? Ex supra et infra scriptis intellegetur non nescio quid subostendi hoc dicto de remotiore doctrina, sed potius inculcari de non admittenda alia praeter eam quam audierat ab ipso, et puto palam, Coram multis, inquit, testibus. Quos multos testes si nolunt ecclesiam intellegi, nihil interest, quando nihil tacitum fuerit quod sub multis testibus proferebatur. Sed nec quia voluit illum haec fidelibus hominibus demandare, qui idonei sint et alios docere, id quoque argumentum occulti alicuius evangelii interpretandum est. Nam cum dicit Haec, de eis dicit de quibus in praesenti scribebat. De occultis autem, ut de absentibus, apud conscientiam non Haec, sed Illa dixisset.
thought_title: The deposit was not a secret doctrine
orientation: Tertullian is answering heretics who claim the apostles taught some things openly and some things secretly, and he is examining Paul's words to Timothy about the deposit.
pass_a_gloss: But, as we have said, it is the same madness, when they confess indeed that the apostles were ignorant of nothing, and did not preach different things among themselves, yet they do not want that they revealed all things to all people, for they say that they entrusted some things openly and to all, some things secretly and to few, because Paul also used this word to Timothy: O Timothy, guard the deposit, and again: Guard the good deposit. What is this deposit, so secret that it is reckoned as belonging to another doctrine? Or is it of that charge about which he says: I commend this charge to you, son Timothy? Likewise of that command about which he says: I charge you before God, who gives life to all things, and Jesus Christ, who bore witness under Pontius Pilate to the good confession, that you keep the command? But what command and what charge? From the things written above and below it will be understood that not some unknown thing is hinted at by this saying about a more hidden doctrine, but rather that it is impressed upon him that no other doctrine is to be admitted besides that which he had heard from him himself, and I think openly: Before many witnesses, he says. If they do not want the church to be understood as these many witnesses, it makes no difference, since nothing was secret that was being brought forward before many witnesses. But not even because he wanted to entrust these things to faithful men, who would be fit to teach others also, is this too to be interpreted as an argument for some hidden gospel. For when he says These things, he speaks about the things about which he was writing at the time. But about hidden things, as about absent things, he would have said not These things but Those things, in the presence of conscience.

choices.why: The glossary requires 'deposit' for depositum, the body of teaching entrusted by Paul to Timothy.
Renders the legal force of denuntiatio as a formal declaration or charge, matching the context of Paul's solemn command.
Praceptum is a direct command or instruction, fitting Paul's imperative to Timothy.
Keeps the literal sense of fidelis as faithful, referring to those who can be trusted with teaching.
Preserves the demonstrative contrast Tertullian draws between present and absent matters, which is the point of his argument.

pass_b_english: But as we have said, it is the same madness when they admit that they have ignored nothing concerning the apostles and did not preach different things among themselves, yet they refuse to believe that the apostles revealed everything to everyone. They claim that some things were entrusted openly and to all, while others were entrusted secretly and to a few, because Paul also used this word to Timothy: "O Timothy, guard the deposit" (1 Timothy 6:20), and again, "Keep the good deposit" (2 Timothy 1:14). What is this deposit, so silent that it is reckoned as another doctrine? Or is it that charge of which he says, "I commend this charge to you, my child Timothy" (1 Timothy 1:18)? Or that command of which he says, "I charge you before God, who gives life to all things, and Jesus Christ, who bore witness before Pontius Pilate to the good confession, to keep the command" (1 Timothy 6:13)? But what command and what charge? From what is written above and below it will be understood that nothing is being hinted at in this saying about some more hidden doctrine, but rather that he is insisting that no other doctrine be admitted besides the one Timothy had heard from him—and I think openly. "Before many witnesses," he says (2 Timothy 2:2). If they do not want the church to be understood by these many witnesses, it makes no difference, since nothing was silent that was brought forth before many witnesses. Nor is the fact that he wanted Timothy to entrust these things to faithful men who would be able to teach others also to be interpreted as an argument for some hidden gospel. For when he says "these things," he is speaking about the things he was writing about at that moment. About hidden things, as about absent things, he would have said "those things," not "these things," in his own conscience.
